# Evidence card — ADHD health information

This skill gives general information from guidance and research. It does not diagnose or advise on treatment.

Use only these claims, within the scope stated. None of them tested this software.

- **CLM-GD-NHS-DIAGNOSIS** (verified against the source): In the UK, ADHD should only be diagnosed by a specialist (e.g. psychiatrist or other appropriately qualified healthcare professional) after a full clinical and psychosocial assessment; a GP may refer to an ADHD specialist.
  Source: [Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NG87)](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87); [ADHD in adults](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/adhd-adults/).
- **CLM-GD-NICE-SDM** (verified against the source): NICE recommends a holistic shared treatment plan and regularly discussing with people with ADHD how they want to be involved in treatment decisions, including benefits and harms of non-drug and drug treatments and their preferences.
  Source: [Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NG87)](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87).
- **CLM-GD-MED-ROUTE** (verified against the source): In the UK, ADHD medicines are started and monitored by an ADHD specialist; questions about how to take a medicine or remember doses can go to a pharmacist, and stopping should be discussed with the doctor first.
  Source: [ADHD in adults](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/adhd-adults/); [Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NG87)](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87); [How and when to take methylphenidate for adults](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methylphenidate-adults/how-and-when-to-take-methylphenidate-for-adults/).
- **CLM-GD-MPH-MISSED** (verified against the source): For methylphenidate (adults), NHS advice for a forgotten dose is to skip it and take the next dose at the usual time, and not to take 2 doses to make up for it; an alarm or a pharmacist can help with remembering.
  Source: [How and when to take methylphenidate for adults](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methylphenidate-adults/how-and-when-to-take-methylphenidate-for-adults/).
- **CLM-GD-MPH-OVERDOSE** (verified against the source): NHS advises getting medical advice after taking more methylphenidate than prescribed even without symptoms (111 online/phone), and calling 999 or going to A&E for a fit/seizure or fast, slow or irregular heartbeat.
  Source: [How and when to take methylphenidate for adults](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methylphenidate-adults/how-and-when-to-take-methylphenidate-for-adults/).
- **CLM-GD-MPH-COMMON** (verified against the source): For methylphenidate in adults, the NHS lists common side effects (more than 1 in 100 people) as headaches, trouble sleeping, loss of appetite (with possible weight loss in the first few months), stomach ache, dry mouth and feeling or being sick, and advises telling a doctor if they bother you or don't go away.
  Source: [Side effects of methylphenidate for adults](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methylphenidate-adults/side-effects-of-methylphenidate-for-adults/).
- **CLM-GD-MPH-URGENT** (verified against the source): For methylphenidate (adults), NHS lists serious side effects to report to a GP or 111 straight away (e.g. mood changes, palpitations, hallucinations, new facial tics) and ones needing 999 or A&E (e.g. chest pain, stroke symptoms, fits, thoughts of harming yourself or others; anaphylaxis -> 999).
  Source: [Side effects of methylphenidate for adults](https://www.nhs.uk/medicines/methylphenidate-adults/side-effects-of-methylphenidate-for-adults/).
- **CLM-GD-NHS-MANAGE** (verified against the source): NHS lists ways to manage adult ADHD including lifestyle changes, work/study adjustments, medicines and talking therapies such as CBT or mindfulness.
  Source: [ADHD in adults](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/adhd-adults/).
- **CLM-GD-NICE-ENV** (verified against the source): NICE describes environmental modifications as changes to the environment, tailored to an assessment of the person's needs, such as changes to seating, lighting and noise, reducing distractions (e.g. headphones), shorter periods of focus with movement breaks, and reinforcing verbal requests with written instructions.
  Source: [Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NG87)](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng87).
- **CLM-RS-CBT-META** (checked against an abstract or summary only): A 2026 meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (Liu et al., Journal of Affective Disorders) reported small-to-moderate improvements with CBT in adults with ADHD for core symptoms (SMD -0.45) and executive function (SMD -0.43), but not for quality of life or self-evaluation. This is about clinician-delivered CBT, not this software.
  Source: [A meta-analysis of the intervention effect of cognitive behavioral therapy on adult ADHD](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jad.2025.121107).
- **CLM-BD-SURVEY** (verified against the source): In one self-selected online survey of 220 adults (most identifying as neurodivergent, ADHD the most common self-identification, no diagnosis required), 186 said they were somewhat more likely or more likely to finish tasks when another person was present, and 108 said more likely. This is self-report with no comparison condition.
  Source: ["It Was Something I Naturally Found Worked and Heard About Later": An Investigation of Body Doubling with Neurodivergent Participants](https://leyabreanna.com/papers/body_double_taccess.pdf).
- **CLM-BD-EEG** (checked against an abstract or summary only): A small 2025 ASSETS study (N=26; neurotypical, medicated ADHD and unmedicated ADHD participants) found no statistically significant differences between body-doubling and solo conditions on ACT reading comprehension or EEG-derived focus and calmness metrics; the authors report no consistent negative impacts and 'promising trends' for unmedicated ADHD participants.
  Source: [Reading Between the Lines: Exploring Body Doubling in ADHD Using EEG](https://doi.org/10.1145/3663547.3759743); [Evaluating the Efficacy of Body Doubling for ADHD Using a Brain-Computer Interface](https://www.ccsc.org/centralplains/2025/talks/talk-poster16/).
- **CLM-BD-MECHANISM** (verified against the source): No source reviewed here tested or established a neurochemical (for example dopamine) mechanism for body doubling. The research papers either do not mention dopamine or list other untested theories (mirror neurons, Hawthorne effect, social facilitation, accountability); consumer pages that mention dopamine or neurotransmitters present it as speculation, an inference from general social-behaviour research, or a claim attributed to a commercial service.
  Source: ["It Was Something I Naturally Found Worked and Heard About Later": An Investigation of Body Doubling with Neurodivergent Participants](https://leyabreanna.com/papers/body_double_taccess.pdf); [A Roadmap of Mixed Reality Body Doubling for Adults with ADHD](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.07851v1); [The ADHD Body Double: A Unique Tool for Getting Things Done](https://add.org/the-body-double/); [Could a Body Double Help You Increase Your Productivity?](https://chadd.org/adhd-weekly/could-a-body-double-help-you-increase-your-productivity/); [ADHD Body Doubling: What It Is and How It Works](https://www.psychcentral.com/adhd/adhd-body-doubling); [What Is 'Body Doubling' and Can It Help With ADHD?](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/body-doubling-for-adhd).
- **CLM-RS-TIME-PERCEPTION** (checked against an abstract or summary only): A 2023 review of a decade of adult ADHD time-perception research (Mette) found few studies and mixed results for time estimation and reproduction: some studies show deficits and others no clear difference. Time-blindness should not be presented as an established universal deficit.
  Source: [Time Perception in Adult ADHD: Findings from a Decade-A Review](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph20043098).

Full register, statuses and limitations: `evidence/claims.yaml` in the source repository. Runtime snapshot: `references/shared/runtime-evidence.md`. No claim has been reviewed by a clinician.
